Good morning, today we will review photosynthesis and prepare the laboratory report.
Open your notebook to page thirty, please.
Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.
The overall equation uses carbon dioxide and water, and it releases oxygen.
The light-dependent reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast.
There, chlorophyll absorbs photons and excites electrons in photosystem two.
Water is split to replace those electrons, and oxygen leaves the plant as a by-product.
The excited electrons travel through an electron transport chain and pump protons.
That proton gradient drives ATP synthase, which produces ATP for the next stage.
The light-independent reactions, also called the Calvin cycle, happen in the stroma.
The enzyme rubisco fixes carbon dioxide into a three-carbon compound.
The cycle uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to build sugars.
One common misconception is that plants only breathe at night; that is not correct.
Plants respire all the time, but during the day photosynthesis usually exceeds respiration.
Another misconception is that the oxygen comes from carbon dioxide; it comes from water.
Let us compare the two stages using a simple table in your notebook.

Include one graph with light intensity on the horizontal axis and oxygen production on the vertical axis.
State your hypothesis in one sentence and describe the control condition.
Report the mean of three trials and mention any outlier you removed.

Choose a real ecosystem and connect at least two cycles to the reactions we studied.

Let us return to the electron transport chain and trace the path of one electron.
Start at photosystem two, follow the carrier proteins, and finish at photosystem one.
Where is the energy used to pump protons, and where is it stored?
Notice that the final electron acceptor is NADP plus, not oxygen.
This is the point most students miss, so write it down and compare with your partner.
Tomorrow we will review cellular respiration and connect it to today's diagram.
Read pages forty-five to forty-eight and bring two written questions.
Remember that the quiz is individual and that late laboratory reports lose ten percent per day.
See you on Thursday, and do not forget to submit the report draft.
Now let us connect photosynthesis to cellular respiration.
Respiration breaks down glucose and releases energy that the cell can use.
It happens in three main stages: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.
Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and does not require oxygen.
The citric acid cycle happens in the mitochondrial matrix.
Oxidative phosphorylation happens at the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Both processes use electron carriers, but they move energy in opposite directions.
Photosynthesis stores energy, while respiration releases it.
A useful comparison is a rechargeable battery: photosynthesis charges it and respiration uses it.
Write this comparison in your notebook and add one example of an organism that does both.
Plants, algae, and some bacteria perform photosynthesis, but all living cells respire.
The laboratory safety rules are mandatory during the next session.
Wear goggles and a lab coat, and never taste any solution.
Label every tube with your group number and the concentration.
Dispose of the used reagents in the container marked for chemical waste.
If a spill happens, stop the experiment and call the instructor immediately.
Record the data in ink, not in pencil, and never erase a measurement.
If you make a mistake, draw one line through the value and write the correction beside it.
The group presentation will use the same rubric as the written report.
One member introduces the question, another explains the method, and the others present the results.
Keep the presentation under five minutes and leave one minute for questions.
Practice the transition between speakers so the talk sounds coherent.
The classroom projector needs a USB-C adapter, and the one at the front desk is available.
Test your slides during the break, not when your group is already presenting.
Friday's quiz will include one graph interpretation question.
Look at the axes, the units, and the trend before writing your answer.
A common mistake is to describe the line without explaining what it means biologically.
Use evidence from the graph and connect it to the reactions we reviewed today.
If the question asks for a hypothesis, write a testable statement rather than a definition.

Good scientific writing is precise, concise, and honest about uncertainty.
Do not hide a result that contradicts your hypothesis; explain it instead.
That is how science works, and it is also how you earn credit for critical thinking.
